title: The US Just Added 172,000 Jobs. A Fed Rate Hike Is Now the Base Case. Here Is What That Means for NRIs.
excerpt: May payrolls crushed forecasts, the unemployment rate held at 4.3 per cent, and the probability of a December rate hike jumped to 70 per cent. The dollar-rupee equation just shifted.
body:
The American economy added 172,000 jobs in May, well above the 85,000 economists had expected, and revised its March and April numbers upward by a combined 93,000. The unemployment rate held at 4.3 per cent for a third straight month. Financial markets immediately recalculated: the probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December jumped to 70 per cent from about 50 per cent before the data landed.

For the estimated 4.8 million Indian professionals and their families living in the United States, the jobs report is not an abstraction. It shapes visa decisions, salary negotiations, interest rates on mortgages and car loans, and the value of the dollar they send home every month.

## The numbers behind the headline

Nonfarm payrolls have now averaged 188,000 jobs per month over the past three months — nearly triple the pace of the same period in 2025. Private sector employment rose by 120,000, with leisure and hospitality adding 70,000 positions, many of them linked to preparations for the FIFA World Cup, which the United States is co-hosting starting June 11.

Healthcare added 35,000 jobs. Construction put on 17,000. Government payrolls rose by 52,000, the most in nearly two years — though federal employment is still down 336,000 from its October 2024 peak after the administration's campaign to shrink the federal workforce.

Annual wage growth actually slowed, to 3.4 per cent from 3.6 per cent in April, which gives the Fed some cover to hold rates even as it digests the stronger hiring numbers. The share of industries reporting employment growth rose to a six-month high of 54.4 per cent.

## The H-1B and tech hiring angle

The report carries a specific tension for Indian tech workers. On one hand, strong job growth signals that companies are hiring, which supports H-1B sponsorship and green card processing. On the other, the sectors adding jobs fastest — hospitality, healthcare, construction — are not the ones that typically sponsor H-1B visas.

Financial activities shed 22,000 jobs and are down 107,000 from their May 2025 peak, reflecting losses for insurance carriers and commercial banking. Air transportation lost 8,700 positions after the collapse of Spirit Airlines. Information and wholesale trade also cut payrolls. These are closer to the white-collar, tech-adjacent sectors where many Indian professionals work.

The labour force participation rate remained at a four-and-a-half-year low of 61.8 per cent. The labour force has shrunk by 1.4 million people since December, in part because the immigration crackdown has reduced the number of workers entering the country. That constraint is artificially lowering the unemployment rate — if more workers were entering, the jobless figure would likely be higher.

## What the Fed does next matters for NRI wallets

The Federal Reserve's next statement is due June 17. If the jobs data nudges the committee toward a rate hike later this year, the consequences ripple outward. Higher US rates strengthen the dollar, which pressures the rupee — already down 6 per cent this year. They raise mortgage rates for Indian families buying homes in America. They increase borrowing costs for Indian companies that have dollar-denominated debt. And they make it more expensive for the RBI to defend the rupee, since the interest rate differential between the two countries would widen.

At the same time, a strong US economy and a firm dollar make remittances more powerful. Every dollar sent to India converts into more rupees. For families who earn in dollars and spend in rupees — which describes a large share of the diaspora — the maths works both ways.

Economists say fiscal stimulus, in the form of tax and import tariff refunds after the Supreme Court struck down sweeping tariffs in February, has cushioned the impact of the Iran conflict on the US economy. Corporate profits have held up, allowing businesses to refrain from large-scale layoffs. But if the war persists, risks to the labour market could emerge.

## The hidden weakness

Buried in the report is a warning. The number of people unemployed for 27 weeks or more rose to 1.99 million, the highest since December 2021. The median duration of unemployment jumped to 11.6 weeks, the longest in nearly five years. People who lose jobs are finding it harder to land new ones.

Vanguard economist Adam Schickling pointed to a specific pattern: unemployment is increasingly concentrated among younger, more educated workers who are staying in the labour force. That demographic overlaps heavily with Indian professionals on H-1B and OPT visas — people who cannot afford extended periods without employment because their immigration status depends on it.

Household disposable income after adjusting for inflation has dropped for three straight months and the savings rate is at a four-year low, as consumers rely on past gains to fund spending. The economy is not weak. But beneath the strong headline number, the foundations are shifting in ways that matter most for the people whose right to remain in the country is tied to their next paycheck.
